primary_topics: Art's four years as personal legal counsel of Senate President Jovito R. Salonga and concurrently counsel of the Liberal Party (1987-1991) -- Salonga's choice of his former student to replace Justice Abraham Sarmiento as personal counsel, the senate president's published observation in the Preface to 'Love God, Serve Man' (1994 PDI volume) of Art's 'radical change... in outlook, his sense of values, his insights, even his conversation,' and Salonga's signal motto-bequest: 'we should never ever forget that it is far more important to aspire even more ardently for things that money cannot buy, like honor, dignity, ethics, character and excellence.'

Two career-defining declined offers preceding the Supreme Court -- (1) Executive Secretary Rafael Salas's late-1960s offer of a Malacañang technical assistant post or judgeship, refused for financial reasons (children's education), and (2) President-elect Fidel V. Ramos's 1992 offer of the Secretary of Justice cabinet seat, refused on three grounds: Art had voted for Salonga, not Ramos; the CBCP-led PPCRV's political neutrality would be put at risk; and Leni had made political office a marriage-contracted veto. Ramos's amused retort: 'Ander de saya ka pala...dalawa na tayo' (I see you're henpecked. That makes two of us).

The three-year arduous JBC screening ordeal (1992-1995) -- President Ramos's pivot from cabinet to Supreme Court appointment, the 1987 Constitution Article VIII Section 8 mandate of the Judicial and Bar Council, Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's adamant opposition to Art's premature presidential pick (despite personal friendship and acknowledged qualification), seven Supreme Court vacancies from 1992-1994, seven consecutive rejections with appellate justices given priority, a former client surfacing with a 25-year-old complaint, and the eventual January 1995 surrender prayer ('Take, oh Lord, all that I am, all that I will ever be. Take my personal ambition, my liberty, my career...').

The Luke 11 / Luke 9 discernment sequence in July-August 1995 -- Justice Jose A.R. Melo's prod after Justice Camilo Quiason's retirement, the 1:00 AM Saturday July 29 wakefulness and two-hour prayer, the parish Sunday July 30 reading of 'Ask and you shall receive, seek and you shall find, knock and the door shall be opened to you' (Luke 11:1-11) producing cold sweat and goosebumps, Art's request for a confirming sign, and the August 6 transfiguration reading 'This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him' (Luke 9:28-36) that he interpreted as direct heavenly command to re-submit his name to the JBC.

The September 1995 JBC reversal and October appointment -- the September 13 attempted exclusion forestalled by one member's plea ('Panganiban's name stay in the list in the meantime'), the September 20 mysteriously unobjected-to inclusion that Art called 'a miracle,' President Ramos's phone call asking 'How did you do it?' -- Art's reply 'Well, sir, I didn't do it. The Lord did. Hallelujah!' -- the BLD community's 'storming of the heavens,' Leni's appeals to the Carmelites and Pink Sisters, and Ramos's eventual appointment call: 'I am the Lord's instrument. He has chosen you, and I therefore appoint you justice of the Supreme Court.'

stances.claim: Art's path to the Supreme Court is presented as the canonical case of providential ascent through humility: seven rejections, a January 1995 surrender prayer, three years of public humiliation including a 25-year-old fabricated complaint, and an explicit conclusion that 'becoming a member of the Supreme Court was not part of God's plan for his life' -- followed by the Luke 11 / Luke 9 discernment sequence reversing the conclusion. The biography treats this as the defining instance of God acting through patient defeat.

Art's hermeneutic of scripture is testimonial and conversational, not academic. Twice in this chapter the Sunday Gospel reading is interpreted as direct personal address from God -- 'Ask and you shall receive...' as instruction, 'Listen to Him' as confirmation. The biography presents this hermeneutic without irony as the reliable method by which a layman could make career decisions.
stances.rhetorical_move: validation of personal scriptural discernment; lectio-as-decision

stances.claim: Three career-defining government offers (Salas, FVR Justice Secretary, Salonga's anticipated Executive Secretary) were all declined or did not materialize before the one that did -- the Supreme Court -- was accepted. The pattern signals an implicit theology of vocation: the right post is the one that does not bend the family veto, does not entail partisan compromise, and is not strategically pursued.
stances.rhetorical_move: vocational pattern recognition through serial non-acceptance

stances.claim: Narvasa's institutional opposition to Art is presented sympathetically -- the JBC chair was defending the very independence of the council from premature presidential influence, and the chapter is careful to note Narvasa's admission that Art was 'qualified.' The friction is structural, not personal, and Art does not become bitter toward Narvasa. The biography models judicial-statesmanship deference.

Leni's marriage-contract political veto is decisive at the cabinet stage -- quoted at length and treated as binding. The chapter establishes that the household partnership has constitutional standing in Art's career discernment. Ramos's amused 'dalawa na tayo' confirms the principle from the highest possible vantage.
stances.rhetorical_move: establishment of marital decision-rule with cross-validation

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 chronicles the arduous and ultimately providential road to Art's appointment as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines. After the 1986 transition, Senator Jovito R. Salonga -- Art's law-school dean turned three-time poll-topping Senate President -- asked his protégé to take over as personal counsel of the Upper House upon Justice Abraham Sarmiento's elevation to the Supreme Court. Concurrently counsel of the Liberal Party, Art served Salonga from 1987 to 1991 and absorbed the motto that would become his own: things money cannot buy -- honor, dignity, ethics, character and excellence. When Salonga lost the 1992 presidential race to General Fidel V. Ramos, the new chief executive -- Art's Rotary Club of Manila co-member -- invited him to dinner at Ambassador Henrietta de Villa's home and at a subsequent one-hour private meeting in Makati offered him Secretary of Justice. Art declined on three grounds: he had voted for Salonga, the PPCRV's political neutrality could be damaged, and Leni had made political office a marriage-contracted veto. He consulted the CBCP, where Archbishop Legazpi feared reputational damage and Bishop Bacani saw strategic value, before Leni's clinching line -- 'we already agreed when we got married many years ago that you could become anything, anything at all, except a politician' -- decided the matter. Ramos, amused ('Ander de saya ka pala...dalawa na tayo'), pivoted to offer the non-political Supreme Court seat instead. But the road to the bench was not direct. Article VIII Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution had created the Judicial and Bar Council precisely to prevent arbitrary presidential picks, and Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa as JBC chair adamantly opposed Art's nomination -- defending the council's independence even while acknowledging Art's qualification. Across seven Supreme Court vacancies from 1992 to 1994, Art's name was submitted to the JBC and seven times he was rejected: appellate justices were given priority, a former client surfaced with a 25-year-old complaint, and the 'others more qualified' rationale was repeatedly cited. Art wept before God, asking 'How long, O God, must I bear these frustrations and the embarrassment of being repeatedly rejected?' but clung to Romans 8:28. In January 1995, broken in spirit, he surrendered: 'Take, oh Lord, all that I am, all that I will ever be. Take my personal ambition, my liberty, my career. Do what you will with them and I will follow whatever You want me to do.' Six months later, after Justice Camilo Quiason's retirement opened the eighth vacancy, Justice Jose A.R. Melo prodded Art to try once more. At 1:00 AM on Saturday July 29, 1995, Art woke and prayed two hours, falling asleep at 4:00 AM without a sign. The next morning at parish Mass, with eyes closed imagining the ascending Jesus, he heard Luke 11:1-11 read -- 'Ask and you shall receive, seek and you shall find, knock and the door shall be opened to you' -- and broke into cold sweat, gasping internally, 'My Lord, are you asking me to persist in my quest?' A week later on August 6, the transfiguration Gospel (Luke 9:28-36) gave the confirmation he had asked for: 'This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him.' He resubmitted his name. On Wednesday August 9, leading the BLD South Sector prayer meeting at St. James School Sucat with Leni, he publicly declared his discernment. On September 13 the JBC nearly excluded him; one unnamed member's plea -- 'let Panganiban's name stay in the list in the meantime' -- kept him in. On September 20, 'by some mysterious reason, no one objected.' For the first time in three years he passed. Ramos called: 'How did you do it?' -- 'Well, sir, I didn't do it. The Lord did. Hallelujah!' Two weeks of intercession by BLD, the Carmelites and Pink Sisters followed before the presidential appointment call: 'I am the Lord's instrument. He has chosen you, and I therefore appoint you justice of the Supreme Court.' On October 18, 1995, before the BLD assembly, Art declared that 'all my actions and all my decisions will only be in accordance with His commandments and His gospel,' pledging to serve 'with fortitude, integrity, competence and prudence.'
